alternative_names: Benjamin Lundy of Mount Pleasant and Baltimore
nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Quaker frontier abolitionism of the old Northwest and the border states; editor and journalist of the formative periodical stage of American antislavery, between the gradualism of the 1820s and the immediatism of the 1830s
literary_identity: An editor, conducting 62 numbers and then hundreds more of a single sustained abolitionist sheet, and therefore chiefly a writer of leading articles, extracts, statistical tables, petitions, correspondence and prospectuses. His independent literary productions are a tract on the colonisation and emancipation questions, his circulars and annual registers of the manumitted, and an enormous body of letters. He invented the American abolitionist periodical as an institution: a monthly carried by agents, sustained by female subscribers, and dependent on the reprinting of British and foreign material.
biography: He was born on 4 January 1789 at Hardwick in Sussex County, New Jersey, the son of Joseph and Eliza Lundy, and was raised in the plain speech and circuit ministry of the Society of Friends on the western frontier. He served an apprenticeship, learned the saddler's trade, and for many years financed his presswork with his own hands and with the proceeds of a small shop. He became an emancipationist through familiarity with the slave country of the border regions, began to contribute to the antislavery press about 1817, and in January 1821 established at Mount Pleasant in Jefferson County, Ohio, on the bank of the Ohio River and immediately opposite slave territory, the Genius of Universal Emancipation. Long afterwards held to have been the first American newspaper wholly devoted to emancipation, it was in fact preceded by Elisha Bates's short-lived Emancipator of Ohio, whose name and subscription lists Lundy bought and merged into his own sheet. He carried the paper to Jonesboro in Tennessee and then in 1824 to Baltimore, where it found its largest circulation and its most dangerous readership, and where for a decade he edited it, appointed agents, and supplied it with reprinted British parliamentary returns, slave-code extracts and accounts of manumission by will. In 1829 he engaged the young William Lloyd Garrison as a corresponding agent and contributor, gave him charge of the memoranda of the department called Plain Fact, and so provided the apprenticeship from which The Liberator issued in the following year. The two men parted over Garrison's immediatism and unconditional refusal of colonisation, Lundy holding to gradual measures, to emancipation financed by the sale of western land, and to the counsel of the Maryland Colonisation interest. He continued the Genius through the crisis years of the 1830s, travelling and publishing to the last, and died at Lowell, Illinois, on 22 August 1839.
literary_profile: His writing is the prose of an editor obliged to fill a sheet monthly at almost no cost: sober, argumentative, heavily indebted to quotation and to table. He worked by accumulation, re-printing British debates, legislative enactments, wills of manumission and Methodist and Quaker resolutions, and framing them with a leading article that stated the case for compensated and staged emancipation. The tone is exhortatory rather than prophetic, and it is characteristically addressed to slaveholders as erring neighbours rather than to the nation as a whole. His most effective prose is in the short factual paragraph, where a single returned fugitive, a shipload of the newly kidnapped or a price-current from a southern market carries its own argument.
stylistic_characteristics: Plain unadorned Quaker diction; heavy use of extract, quotation and tabulated statement; a modest first-person editorial voice that reports his own journeys and receipts; moral argument conducted by enumeration of cases; long running titles and departmental headings; earnest, repetitive address to the conscience of the border-state reader; little irony except in the Plain Fact memoranda compiled by his sub-editor.
intellectual_concerns: The extension of slavery into the western states and its effect upon free labour; the education and moral elevation of the free coloured population; gradual emancipation, compensated manumission by will and the purchase of land for the settled freedom of the manumitted; the danger of the slave trade's renewal after the abolition of importation; the use of periodical publicity and female subscription as the engine of reform; the kinship of American and British emancipation, and the example of the West Indian apprenticeship debate.
historical_significance: He made American abolition a continuing organised press enterprise rather than an occasional address. For a dozen years the Genius was the movement's record and its correspondence network, and through it Lundy trained and launched William Lloyd Garrison, whose first abolitionist editorship was in Lundy's Baltimore office. His papers document the transition from the founding generation's gradualism to the immediatism of 1831 and later, and the disputes in which he was defeated, over colonisation, over the union of the churches and over the sinfulness of slaveholding, defined the programme of the movement that succeeded him. He is justly called the father of American organized abolition.
major_influences: The Society of Friends and its ministry of travel and plain speech
the British and Foreign Slave Trade abolition literature which he reprinted
the example of the Ohio and Tennessee manumission societies
Elisha Bates's Emancipator of Ohio
the writings of the American Colonisation controversy
the public of female abolitionist subscribers whose donations sustained his press
biographical_uncertainty: His birthplace is disputed in popular account: the weight of authority places it at Hardwick or in Sussex County, New Jersey, while a minority of local and school tradition gives a Pennsylvania birth, and the family's settlement on the upper Ohio is variously dated. The exact chronology of the Genius is complicated by changes of title, place and frequency, and surviving runs are incomplete, so that particular numbers and their contents cannot always be tied to a fixed date. His share in the authorship of material printed under his editors name, as distinct from that contributed by Garrison and by corresponding agents, is not separable in every case.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American, of the Philadelphia theatre; the republican historical drama and melo-drama of the early national stage, and the first significant American dramatist of the Pocahontas and Indian-captivity legend
literary_identity: A playwright of ten plays, comic and tragical, written for the stock companies of Philadelphia and afterwards produced in New York and London, together with adapted comedies, verses and civic odes. His forms are the afterpiece and the melo-drama, the domestic comedy of manners and the historical tragedy, and he works characteristically with the musical interlude, the tableau and the moral epilogue.
biography: He was born on 17 June 1784 at Annapolis in Maryland, of a family of military standing, the son of the man whom the Philadelphia finding aid for his papers styles General John Barker, and he was brought up in Philadelphia, the city of the American stage. He held a commission in the artillery and served with the army through the second war with England, rising to the rank of major, and he carried into public life the reputation of an officer of the regular establishment. His first printed play, The Indian Princess; or, La Belle Sauvage, was published at Philadelphia by the firm of Palmer in 1808, the year of its first performance on the Philadelphia stage, and it made his name: it is the first American play upon an Indian theme and the first successful Pocahontas drama, and in December 1820 it was produced at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, the first play of an American author to reach that house in the nineteenth century. He followed it with comedy and melo-drama, a translated or adapted piece entitled How to Try a Lover issued in the dramatic repositories of 1817, and the domestic comedy Tears and Smiles, which is usually counted among the contributing forms of the stage Yankee. Superstition; or, the Fanatic Father, a tragedy of monastic guilt printed in 1824, was long accounted the best of his serious dramas and held the repertory in the United States. Public office succeeded the stage: he represented Philadelphia interests, and in the years 1819 and 1820 he served as mayor of the city, after which he continued to write occasional verse and prose for civic occasions. He died on 9 March 1858, having been remembered throughout his later life as the soldier, manager and magistrate who had first put the American Indian legend on the public stage.
literary_profile: His drama is constructed for effect and for the capabilities of a stock company, and his best scenes are those of spectacle, capture and deliverance, in which moral argument is carried by situation rather than by speech. The Indian Princess treats Pocahontas as a principle of natural generosity and of converted gentleness, and its plea for mercy between the strong and the weak is delivered in the verse and song proper to the afterpiece and in a diction of buoyant sentimental declaration. His comedy of Philadelphia life depends upon assumption, mistaken identity and the satire of manners, while his tragedy of Superstition attacks monastic fanaticism and priestly power with the plain Protestant vehemence proper to the popular stage. He prefixes prefaces to his printed plays in which he defends the treatment of historical character, an early instance of the American dramatist's claim to be read.
stylistic_characteristics: Verse and song intermixed with prose dialogue; tableau, entrance and explosion as the units of structure; declarative sentiment in long moral period; heroic-couplet dignity for Indian and heroic characters; comic dialogue built on mistake, assumption and the manners of Philadelphia society; anti-Catholic polemic in the tragedy; an epilogue or moral gloss addressed directly to the audience.
intellectual_concerns: The treatment of the American Indian in legend and in history and the possibility of generosity between races; national subject matter for a national theatre, and the claim of American drama to the London stage; the tyranny of superstition, monastic power and the fanatic father; the ethics of capture, adoption and deliverance; gentility, manners and civic virtue in the early republic; the soldier's and the magistrate's duty to the republic.
historical_significance: He fixed the Pocahontas story in its American dramatic form and made the Indian Princess a stock piece of the nineteenth-century stage, on which the legend passed into pictorial, juvenile and later cinematic treatment. His production at Drury Lane in 1820 was a milestone in the transatlantic recognition of American drama, and his plays are the principal evidence that the early national theatre could treat colonial history as national myth. As a soldier and mayor of Philadelphia he also illustrates the union of letters, military service and civic office characteristic of the generation after the revolution.
major_influences: The Philadelphia and New York stock theatre of the early republic and its acting managers
the English melo-drama and afterpiece tradition with its songs, spectacles and moral epilogues
the colonial histories of Virginia and the Pocahontas legend as delivered by the chroniclers
the sentimental comedy of the British stage
the anti-popish and domestic tragedy current in the American repertory
biographical_uncertainty: The Annapolis birthplace rests upon the standard biographical account, beginning with Musser's study of 1929 and repeated by the later encyclopaedias, and no registry record is cited for it; the identity and rank of his father are reported only in finding-aid style. The dates of first performance and of publication of several of his plays differ in the extant playbills and editions, and the order and attribution of his ten dramas, especially of the adaptations issued in the dramatic repositories, are unsettled. The precise offices he held in the artillery and the chronology of his mayoralty vary between civic memoirs.

alternative_names: Captain John Gabriel Stedman of the Scots Brigade
birthplace: Dendermonde in the Austrian Netherlands (now Belgium); earlier authority gives Antigua
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Anglo-Dutch; an officer of the Scottish brigade in the service of the Dutch Republic writing in English; the colonial testimony and travel-narrative wing of abolitionism, and a forerunner of the Romantic documentary horror narrative
literary_identity: A journal-keeper and memoirist rather than a literary professional. His single great work is a first-person narrative of five years of forest warfare in Surinam, interleaved with natural history, plans for the reform of colonial government, verse inscriptions and a sustained indictment of plantation slavery. He also left projected religious and educational writings, and a body of drawings which were engraved to illustrate his own text.
biography: He was born in 1744 at Dendermonde in the Austrian Netherlands, now in Belgium, the son of Robert Stedman, a Scotsman who held a commission in the service of the Dutch Republic; earlier biographers, finding him afterwards in English-speaking colonies, reported his birth at Antigua and the older story of a West Indian origin persists in some accounts. He followed the family profession into the Scots Brigade in Dutch service and in 1772 answered a call for volunteers to act against the revolted negroes of Surinam, the Bosjes or Boni maroons who had won territory in the interior from the plantation colony. He served seven campaigning seasons between 1772 and 1777 in forest and river warfare against these maroon settlements, and kept during them the journals from which his book was made. While at Paramaribo he lived with Joanna, an enslaved woman of mixed descent whom he had bought, loved and intended to emancipate; the record of her two public whippings for theft, the second of them inflicted with a halter and a bit, is the most terrible single passage in his narrative and is written in her defence and in his own condemnation. Broken in health and unable to complete the purchase of Joanna's freedom, he quitted the service and returned to Europe, where for nearly twenty years he lived in London in straitened circumstances, occupied with religious and educational projects and with the reduction of his Surinam journals to a fair copy. He wrote the narrative out in 1790 and sent the manuscript to Joseph Johnson, the London publisher. The Narrative of a Five Years' Expedition, against the Revolted Negroes of Surinam, in Guiana, on the Wild Coast of South America, from the Year 1772 to 1777 appeared in London in 1796 in stately volumes with a series of engraved and aquatint plates, and Stedman died on 7 March 1797, within a year of its publication, still grieved by the fate of Joanna and of the son he had succeeded in obtaining freedom for and educating in England.
literary_profile: The narrative alternates the campaigning journal, the natural-history survey and the abolitionist charge, and its peculiar power comes from the confession of an implicated insider. Stedman describes punishments he has witnessed, sanctioned or failed to prevent, with an eye for the technology of the scene, the number of lashes, the instruments and the speech of the victim. He draws the maroons as brave, articulate and politically able, and the planters and their managers as vain, lazy and cruel, an inversion that made the book a repository of argument for British abolitionists. The 1796 printed text was revised and abridged by an editor before and after the author's death, and the tone of the surviving manuscript, first transcribed entire in the twentieth century, is more frank, more religiously eccentric and more self-accusing than the printed version.
stylistic_characteristics: Precise, dreadful enumeration of bodies, wounds and instruments; a journal's chronology of dates, marches and weather; apostrophic outburst and lament for Joanna; embedded verse epitaphs and inscriptions; natural-history nomenclature placed beside scenes of torture; an unconcealed first-person narrator who reports his own weakness; elaborate period punctuated by exclamation; drawing and engraving treated as evidence coequal with the written account.
intellectual_concerns: The morality of resistance by the enslaved and the character of maroon societies; the cruelty of colonial jurisprudence and of corporal punishment; the complicity of the officer, the witness and the owner; the relation of Christianity to plantation government; schemes for the amelioration and eventual emancipation of the colonial slave; the natural history and geography of tropical America; the fate of mixed unions and of the children of the enslaved.
historical_significance: His narrative of 1796 supplied British and continental abolitionism with some of its most effective evidence and some of its most circulated images, and its plates, designed by the author and engraved by William Blake and others, became standard antislavery illustrations. Read alongside the speeches and enquiries of the 1790s, it carried the case against Dutch and British colonial slavery into the drawing room and made the treatment of Joanna a canonical instance of the argument that slavery degrades the master. Its complicated textual history, from an edited and abridged 1796 print to the first transcription of the 1790 manuscript in the late twentieth century, is a central case study in how colonial testimony was shaped by abolitionist publishers.
major_influences: The Dutch Scots Brigade and its regimental memoir tradition
the journals of eighteenth-century natural history and travel
his own drawings and the school of sentimental pictorial narrative
the devotional and prophetic strain of his religious projects
the abolitionist circle of Joseph Johnson's London publishing house
the African testimony of Olaudah Equiano, published by the same house
biographical_uncertainty: The place of his birth is unsettled: recent authority derives from Dutch and Belgian records and gives Dendermonde in the Austrian Netherlands, while older English accounts give Antigua, and his mother's family and his education remain ill documented. The extent and direction of editorial alteration in the 1796 printed text, and the identity and method of the friend who prepared the second volume from his papers, are disputed among the scholars of the manuscript. The dates of Joanna's life, her death and the success of Stedman's efforts to manumit her cannot be fixed from his own text alone, and the chronology of the return to Europe varies between accounts.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; New England Unitarian letters turned to reform; the woman of letters who joined fiction, children's editing, domestic economy and abolitionist argument in a single career, and a founder of the American sentimental reform novel
literary_identity: An extraordinarily various writer: novelist of colonial Indian scenes, historian for children, editor of the first American periodical for the young, authoress of the standard American household manual, essayist, letter writer, poet of occasional verse and, after 1833, the most widely read white female advocate of immediate emancipation. She wrote for the nursery, the kitchen, the subscription list and the platform, and she regarded these as one province.
biography: She was born Lydia Maria Francis at Medford, Massachusetts, on 11 February 1802, the youngest of the children of David Francis and Susannah Rand Francis, and she lost her mother while still a little girl. The household was of the middling trades and the formation of her mind was largely her own, aided by an elder brother who entered the Unitarian ministry and whose library and example gave her her first sense of a religious vocation in letters. She kept a school at Medford, and at twenty-two she published anonymously a short romance of the colonial period, Hobomok, which sold well and established her as a writer of Indian and frontier subject matter; it was followed in 1825 by The Rebels; or, Boston before the Revolution, a domestic history of the town on the eve of resistance to the crown. In 1826 she founded and conducted the Juvenile Miscellany, the first periodical printed in the United States for children, which she edited for several years and by which she was made known to families across the states. On 3 October 1828 she married David Lee Child, a lawyer of Massachusetts who afterwards turned to farming, and in 1829 she published The Frugal Housewife, afterwards known as The American Frugal Housewife and dedicated to those who are not ashamed of economy, the most successful of her books and for generations a standard of New England household management. The First Settlers of New-England, a history of the Pequot and Narraganset wars related by a father to his children, appeared in 1828. Her reading of the colonial and contemporary treatment of Native Americans prepared her for the great change of her life: An Appeal in Favor of That Class of Americans Called Africans, published at Boston in 1833, cost her friends, subscribers and her children's readership, and made her a central figure of the new immediatism. She continued to write for the cause, edited the National Anti-Slavery Standard in the forties, advocated the rights of women and of the freedpeople, adopted a ward of the race she had befriended, and died at Wayland, Massachusetts, on 20 October 1880.
literary_profile: Her characteristic form is the address to a beginner: the child, the bride, the young reader of history, the conscience newly awakened. She writes with an assumption of intimacy and with a talent for the illustrative anecdote, and her historical fiction and her juvenile books alike proceed by homely detail, dated event and moral gloss rather than by plot of great force. Her abolitionist writing shifts the method of the household book into argument, accumulating evidence, precedent and appeal in orderly chapters, and her letters and memoirs carry the same plain unaffected manner. She is at her best where instruction and feeling are made one, and her worst where the moral takes the place of observation.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear simple syntax with a conversational warmth; direct address to the reader, often as child or housekeeper; inventory and prescription, lists of economies and of facts; historical romance relieved by moral reflection; scriptural and providential cadence inherited from Unitarian preaching; sentiment restrained by practical good sense; a tendency to apostrophe and reproach in the polemic writing of the 1830s.
intellectual_concerns: The education and moral formation of children; the economy and dignity of household labour and the competence of women in domestic management; the writing of American history for the young and the justice owed to the first possessors of the land; slavery as a national sin and a question of immediate duty; the condition and capacity of women; the union of literary profession and reform; the character of republican nationhood tested by its treatment of subject races.
historical_significance: She created the American children's periodical, wrote the most widely used American domestic manual of her generation, and, by the Appeal of 1833, gave the immediatist movement in the United States its first comprehensive statement from a woman's pen and its most influential book among the reading public. Her career shows the passage of New England women's letters from fiction and instruction into political polemic, and the price paid by a woman who made that passage publicly. Later writings for the freedpeople and for women's rights place her at the opening of a reform tradition that ran to the civil war and beyond.
major_influences: Unitarian preaching and the example of her brother the clergyman
the colonial annals and Indian legends of New England and the historical romance of her own generation
the eighteenth-century conduct and housekeeping books
the Quaker and British antislavery literature of the 1820s
the testimony and organisation of the Garrisonian circle and of the female antislavery societies
biographical_uncertainty: The account of her father's trade and of her mother's death varies between biographies, and the dates and conduct of her schoolkeeping at Medford are slight in the record. The first edition of The Rebels is anonymous, and her authorship of material in the Juvenile Miscellany is not always separable from that of her contributors. Her titles were several times re-named in reissue, and the date of the first series of the Frugal Housewife and of the Miscellany's suspension is variously printed. The extent of her share in the editorial management of the Anti-Slavery Standard, and the details of her later religious and spiritualist readings, depend upon memoir rather than upon documents.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Black sermon and public-address tradition of the Northern free communities; the Garrisonian press of the 1830s and the religious oratory of the African Methodist and Baptist circles of Boston
literary_identity: A preacher-speaker and essayist whose literary unit is the address. Her canon is small and of a single piece: a tract of religious and racial counsel, four public lectures delivered in Boston, a collected volume of meditations and essays, and the later contributions to the Black press. She writes in the idiom of the sermon, with scripture, reproach, prophecy and appeal, but she is also the earliest American woman to argue in print for the education, the economic improvement and the public voice of her own sex and colour.
biography: She was born Maria Miller at Hartford, Connecticut, in 1803, in the free Black community of the town; orphaned in childhood and bound out as a servant in a clergyman's household, she had such schooling as the Sabbath schools of Hartford afforded and taught herself to read and write with diligence. She worked in service from her earliest years and passed some years in New York City, and on 10 August 1826, in Boston, she married James W. Stewart, a Black shipping agent who had served in the United States navy during the war of 1812. His death three years later left her a widow without the property her husband's will was intended to secure for her, defrauded by white claimants and dependent again upon teaching and housework. In Boston she joined the religious and mutual-aid circles of the free Black community, was moved by a conversion experience to labour for the elevation of her people, and came under the notice of William Lloyd Garrison, who printed her first written address, Religion and the Pure Principles of Morality, the Sure Foundation on Which We Must Build, in the columns of The Liberator and in tract form, commonly dated 1831. She then began the public career for which she is remembered, addressing the African American Female Intelligence Society on 28 April 1832, delivering at Franklin Hall on 21 September 1832 the lecture known as Why Sit Ye Here and Die, and speaking twice more in 1833, all before mixed audiences of women and men. The addresses, with a sermon and meditations, were gathered in 1833 as Meditations from the Pen of Mrs. Maria W. Stewart, printed for her by Garrison's friends. The criticism passed upon a woman who spoke in public determined her to withdraw from the platform; she continued to teach, contributed prose to the press of her own community in later decades, lived finally in the capital, and died at Freedmen's Hospital, Washington, on 17 December 1879.
literary_profile: Her prose is oral by design and religious by premise. The sermon form supplies her structure, an exposition of text, an application to the audience's condition and a closing summons, and she fills it with statistical and historical instance, with the examples of biblical women and with pointed reproach to men who permit their wives and daughters to sit unlettered. The rhetorical question and the apostrophe carry her argument, and her most powerful writing turns upon the shame of inaction rather than upon description of injury. The volume of 1833 shows her range, passing from exhortation to enterprise, to education, to patience under wrong, and its prefatory matter explains and defends her own public speech.
stylistic_characteristics: Preaching rhythms with a woman's first-person authority; dense scriptural quotation and typology; sustained interrogative address, why sit ye here and die; direct rebuke of the audience's sloth joined to tenderness for its suffering; parallelism and triadic emphasis; moral analogy drawn from nature, from the classical and sacred past and from the everyday economy of Northern Black life; a print style shaped by oral delivery and by the Liberator's columns.
intellectual_concerns: The religious duty of self-improvement and of public speech; the education of Black women and children as the foundation of racial elevation; the moral and economic uplift of the free coloured community; the complicity of the North with slavery and the shame of passive waiting; Providence, race and national destiny in the American republic; the rights and obligations of women as teachers, writers and speakers; temperance, industry and the dignity of labour.
historical_significance: She was the first American-born woman known to lecture on political, racial and religious subjects to mixed audiences of women and men, and one of the first to publish such writing, and her pamphlet and addresses of 1831 to 1833 open the literature of Black women's reform in the United States. Her public career marks the entrance of African American women into Garrisonian abolitionism, and her defence of her own voice supplies the founding argument of a tradition running through the anti-lynching and suffrage oratory of later decades. The recovery of her texts in modern scholarship has established her as a central figure of American religious and feminist letters.
major_influences: The Black church and the African Methodist and Baptist preaching traditions of New England and New York
the Sabbath school and mutual-aid societies of the free coloured communities
the published sermons and oratory of the American revivals
the women's mutual-aid, literary and antislavery societies of Boston and Philadelphia
the patronage and press of William Lloyd Garrison and of The Liberator
biographical_uncertainty: The month of her birth at Hartford, the free or enslaved condition of her parents before her own birth, and the exact chronology of her childhood servitude are variously reported. The pamphlet of Religion and the Pure Principles of Morality is dated 1831 by some authorities and 1832 by others, and its first printing, in the Liberator or in tract form, cannot always be sequenced. The date of her husband's death, the details of the litigation over his estate, and the years of her teaching in New York and Baltimore are imperfectly documented, and the record of her last decades in Washington rests mainly on institutional notice.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Bermudian and Antiguan by enslavement, published in London; the first enslaved Black woman to give her testimony to the press in Britain, and a founding text of the women's slave narrative and of British immediatist agitation
literary_identity: An oral narrator rather than a writer. Her text was spoken and transcribed by Susanna Strickland and arranged and annotated by Thomas Pringle, and it appears in print as a first-person testimony with an editor's supplement, an appendix of documents and the appended narrative of Asa-Asa. Her literary form is the witness statement: a continuous account of hire, labour, punishment and endurance addressed to a public assumed to be ignorant and required to be convinced.
biography: She was born in Bermuda about 1 October 1788, of enslaved parents, and she grew up in the hired-out childhoods of the island's poor, passed from holder to holder and put to domestic, field and out-of-door labour as a child. She describes with exactness the punishments inflicted for small faults, the injuries which left her permanently damaged in one eye and in her limbs, and the sequence of sales and bequests by which she came finally into the property of John Adams Wood, an Antiguan mariner, on whose Antigua estate and in whose household she worked for many years. When Wood travelled with his family to London in 1828 she found herself in a country where the law did not compel the service of the enslaved, left his household, maintained herself in the capital and came under the protection of antislavery friends there. Through the introduction of those friends she reached Thomas Pringle, the secretary of the London Anti-Slavery Society, who arranged that Susanna Strickland should take down her account, and The History of Mary Prince, a West Indian Slave. Related by Herself, with a Supplement by the Editor, was published in London in 1831 at the charge of the Society, priced within the reach of the local auxiliary societies and of the women's subscriptions. Three editions were printed in that year and its evidence of flogging, of the punishment of expectant women and of the exposure of the sick in the field was attacked with fury by proslavery writers in Edinburgh and London. In 1833 Pringle recovered damages for libel, and Wood at once brought his own action against him, which the editor could not effectively answer because West Indian witnesses were unattainable; the threat of further suits stopped a projected fourth edition, and Pringle and his associates worked to secure Prince's freedom and her support. She disappears from the record after 1833, and the place and date of her death are unknown.
literary_profile: The History is built as testimony and its eloquence is that of exact statement. She names places, holders, overseers, instruments and numbers of lashes, and she dates her sufferings by the hurricanes, the droughts and the deaths that marked them. Where argument seems required she does not argue but reports, so that the reader supplies the verdict, and where grief seems required she turns at once to the condition of other women, to the mothers parted from their children and to the workers killed by over-exertion. The book is frankly devotional, holding to the hope of heaven and refusing to let Christian profession excuse the plantation, and its closing appeal to the mothers and women of England is among the most effectual passages of abolitionist prose.
stylistic_characteristics: First-person witness narration, direct and unhedged; naming and numbering as the principal rhetorical device; short declarative sentences broken by exclamations of appeal; biblical cadence and lament; recurring address to the pity and conscience of the reader; an unsentimental register for bodily injury; editorial frames, notes and documents interposed around a voice that remains recognisably individual.
intellectual_concerns: Slavery as property in the body, in women's labour and in children; the exposure of tropical field and household service to metropolitan readers; the failure of Christian masters and the authority of an enslaved woman's own word; marriage, motherhood and the insecurity of the enslaved family; the freedom obtained in England and the legal doubts attending it; the complicity of a public that buys slave-grown produce and reads attacks on the narrative.
historical_significance: Her book of 1831 was the first narrative of a woman's experience of slavery published in Britain and one of the most effective pieces of evidence produced by the immediatist campaign before the abolition act of 1833; three editions appeared in its first year, it was reviewed and reprinted transatlantically, and it carried the condition of colonial slavery into ordinary reading. The litigation of 1833 which followed it laid bare the legal vulnerability of abolitionist publication, cost Pringle his position and suppressed a projected edition. Her text is now a foundational work of Caribbean and feminist literary history, a national text in Bermuda, and the earliest canonical instance of the enslaved woman's voice in English.
major_influences: The oral testimony and preaching traditions of the enslaved communities of Bermuda and Antigua
the missionary instruction recorded in her own account
the London Anti-Slavery Society and its demand for evidence
the transcription of Susanna Strickland and the editorial method of Thomas Pringle
the earlier published narratives of the middle passage and of West Indian field labour
biographical_uncertainty: Her birth is given as 1788 in Bermuda by the weight of modern authority, the day fixed to about the first of October by the narrative's own statement of her age, while a few accounts print 1787. Nothing certain is known of her death or of her whereabouts after 1833, and whether she remained in Britain or returned to the West Indies; no contemporary likeness of her survives. The succession of her early holders is variously reported, and the degree to which Pringle and Strickland shaped her dictated words is disputed, the text being testimony taken down rather than writing composed by its subject.
